rows.verified: Acetylene is extremely flammable and can form an explosive atmosphere in air or oxygen.
Employers must assess acetylene fire and explosion risks under DSEAR and implement suitable controls where explosive atmospheres may occur.
Compressed acetylene can decompose explosively under some conditions even without air or oxygen.
Acetylene should be used by trained people with equipment designed and maintained for the process.

An acetylene cylinder heated in a fire can remain at risk of explosion for hours; HSE advises immediate evacuation around the cylinder and contact with the fire and rescue service rather than moving or venting it.
Oxygen use can create fire and explosion hazards through oxygen enrichment, requiring controls over leaks, equipment condition and work practices.
Oxygen equipment requires suitable maintenance and additional precautions in confined spaces.
Compressed-air systems require controls for overpressure, blockages, overheating, plant failure, inspection, maintenance and operator training.
Compressed-gas risk depends on gas properties, pressure, cylinder and valve condition, storage, ventilation, ignition sources, fire exposure, equipment compatibility and handler competence.
Compressed-gas evidence is gas-, cylinder-, equipment-, task- and condition-specific and is not an exact parcel-level fire, explosion or injury probability.
A permit-to-work is a formal system stating what work is to be done, when it will occur and which parts of the plant or workplace are safe.
A responsible person should assess the work and verify safety at each stage.
People doing the permitted work sign to confirm that they understand the hazards and necessary precautions.
Permit systems provide structured communication between site management, plant supervisors, operators and the people carrying out the work.
Typical permit-controlled activities include hot work, vessel entry, cutting hazardous pipework and work requiring electrical or mechanical isolation.
A permit-to-work does not replace a robust risk assessment; it communicates and implements the assessment at the work location.
Effective permits define roles, provide clear hazard and control information, coordinate simultaneous work and maintain safe shift handover.
Before equipment is returned to service, the permit process requires confirmation that the work is complete and the equipment is ready for normal use.
Permit effectiveness depends on the specific hazard, isolation standard, competence, simultaneous operations, shift handover, document clarity, monitoring and close-out discipline.
Permit-to-work evidence is activity-, hazard-, plant-, isolation- and management-specific and is not an exact parcel-level accident probability.
